title: From Page to Practice
outcomeStatement: By the end of this, you'll be able to use what you read instead of only recognising it.
drawnFrom: Make It Stick — Peter Brown, Henry Roediger, Mark McDaniel

practices.title: Close the book and write
practices.body: Name the last book you finished. Without opening it or any notes, write everything you remember — ideas, arguments, anything. Give it five minutes. Don't check anything yet.

practices.title: Now open it
practices.body: Look at the contents page and your highlights. Write what you missed. The gap between what you felt you knew and what you could produce is the whole problem this journey is about.

practices.title: Why do you keep reading books you don't use?
practices.body: There's usually a reason, and it's usually not laziness.

practices.title: Explain it to a twelve-year-old
practices.body: Pick one idea you've read recently. Write it in your own words as if explaining to a bright twelve-year-old — no jargon from the book. Where the explanation goes vague is where you don't actually understand it.

practices.behavior: one sentence on what you'd do differently because of it
practices.title: One sentence, every time
practices.body: Not a summary. A consequence. If nothing would change, that's a valid and useful answer to write down.

practices.title: The feeling of understanding
practices.body: Today, notice each time you feel like you've understood something you're reading or watching. Then quietly check: could you explain it right now, out loud, with the page closed? Just count the times the answer is no.
practices.noticeFor: feeling fluent without being able to explain it

practices.title: Pull something back from a month ago
practices.body: Pick something you learned about a month ago. Write what you remember before checking. Retrieving something with effort strengthens it far more than re-reading it comfortably.

practices.title: The smallest possible version
practices.body: Take one idea you've read and do the tiniest real version of it today. Not plan it — do it. Ten minutes. Write what happened, including if it didn't work.

practices.title: Which ideas do you collect because they're comfortable rather than useful?
practices.body: Some things we save because they confirm who we already are.

practices.title: Put two unrelated things together
practices.body: Take two things you're currently learning that have nothing to do with each other. Write one place where they touch, or where one contradicts the other. Mixing subjects feels harder and works better than blocking them.

practices.title: Teach it out loud
practices.body: Explain one idea to a real person in under three minutes, without notes. Watch where you stumble — that's the part you don't have yet. Write down where it broke.

practices.cue: When you're tempted to start a new book
practices.behavior: don't — until you've used something from the last one
practices.title: Finish using before you start reading
practices.body: Starting the next book is the most comfortable way to avoid applying the last one.

practices.title: Space it out on purpose
practices.body: Pick three ideas worth keeping. For each, write a date in the next month when you'll test yourself on it, with the book closed. Put the dates somewhere you'll actually see them.

practices.title: What can you do now that you couldn't two weeks ago?
practices.body: Read your day 1 entry first — the one you wrote with the book closed. Then answer in terms of things you can do, not things you know.
